summary: EVPN (RFC 7432) gives intra-subnet connectivity in MPLS and NVO networks. This document defines a new EVPN route type for advertising IP prefixes, for networks that need inter-subnet connectivity for systems that do not run dynamic routing, and gives some use-case examples.

plainLanguage.summary: Not every device in a data center can speak a routing protocol. This document adds a new kind of route that lets the network announce whole groups of addresses on their behalf.

subtitle: A new EVPN route type, RT-5, that lets a data center network advertise whole IP subnets for systems that cannot speak routing protocols.

tldr.problem: EVPN already advertises the MAC and IP addresses of individual hosts, but data centers also need to advertise whole subnets that sit behind virtual appliances and other systems that do not run dynamic routing.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9136 defines EVPN route type 5 (RT-5), which carries an IP prefix and optionally an Overlay Index, a gateway IP, an Ethernet Segment Identifier or a MAC address, that the receiver resolves recursively to find the egress device.
tldr.outcome: Prefixes are decoupled from MAC advertisements, so a failover such as a floating IP moving between appliances needs one route update instead of thousands, and the RFC 7432 procedures stay unchanged.

facts.label: IP prefix length range
facts.value: 0 to 32 for IPv4, 0 to 128 for IPv6

today: RFC 9136 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2021, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It works together with RFC 9135 and builds on RFC 7432.

sections.title: What the New Route Type Is For
sections.content:
The BGP MPLS-based Ethernet VPN (EVPN) mechanism of RFC 7432 provides a flexible control plane that allows intra-subnet connectivity in an MPLS and/or Network Virtualization Overlay network. In some networks there is also a need for dynamic and efficient inter-subnet connectivity across Tenant Systems and end devices that can be physical or virtual and do not necessarily participate in dynamic routing protocols. This document defines a new EVPN route type for the advertisement of IP prefixes and explains some use-case examples where it is used.

The framework for data center network virtualization (RFC 7365) requires the Network Virtualization Edge devices to provide Layer 2 and Layer 3 virtualized network services in multi-tenant data centers, and RFC 8365 discusses the use of EVPN as the technology of choice for Layer 2, or intra-subnet, services. This document, together with RFC 9135, specifies the use of EVPN for Layer 3, or inter-subnet, connectivity services.

RFC 9135 describes how the MAC and IP addresses encoded in EVPN route type 2 routes are used not only to populate the MAC Virtual Routing and Forwarding tables and the overlay ARP tables, but also IP-VRF tables, with the encoded tenant host routes. In some cases EVPN may advertise IP prefixes and so provide aggregation in the IP-VRF tables, as opposed to propagating individual host routes. This document complements those scenarios and defines how EVPN may be used to advertise IP prefixes. Interoperability between EVPN and Layer 3 VPN IP Prefix routes is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: EVPN already tells the network about individual machines. This adds a way to tell it about whole subnets, for the many devices in a data center that cannot speak routing protocols themselves.

sections.title: Inter-Subnet Connectivity in a Data Center
sections.content:
RFC 7432 is used as the control plane for a network virtualization overlay solution in data centers, where the NVE devices can be located in hypervisors or top-of-rack switches. Several kinds of tenant system attach to the broadcast domains of that solution by attachment circuits.

A tenant system may be a virtual machine that generates traffic from its own MAC and IP addresses. It may also be a virtual appliance that forwards traffic to and from IP addresses of different end devices sitting behind it. These appliances can be firewalls, load balancers, NAT devices, other appliances, or virtual gateways with virtual routing instances, and they do not necessarily participate in dynamic routing protocols, so they rely on the EVPN NVEs to advertise the routes on their behalf. In all these cases the appliance forwards traffic to other tenant systems using its own source MAC, but the source IP is the one associated with the end device behind it, or a translated IP address from a public NAT pool.

The same IP address and endpoint can exist behind two tenant systems. One example is an appliance resiliency mechanism where a virtual or floating IP is owned by one of two appliances running the resiliency protocol, the Master appliance; the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol is one particular example. Another is a multihomed subnet, where the same subnet is connected to two appliances. These appliances also do not always have their own IP interface connected to the EVPN NVE, and Layer 2 firewalls are examples of appliances without an IP interface.

For a broadcast domain to which an ingress NVE is attached, the Overlay Index is defined as an identifier that the ingress NVE requires in order to forward packets to a subnet or host in a remote subnet. It is a next hop in the overlay address space, and it can be an IP address, a MAC address, or an Ethernet Segment Identifier. When advertised along with an IP prefix, the Overlay Index requires a recursive resolution to find out the egress NVE to which the packets need to be sent.

All of these data center use cases require inter-subnet forwarding. The individual host routes and subnets must be advertised from the NVEs, since appliances and virtual machines do not participate in dynamic routing protocols, and they may be associated with an Overlay Index that can be an appliance IP address, a floating IP address, a MAC address, or an ESI.
sections.plainLanguage: Many devices in a data center sit behind appliances that hold the routing on their behalf. The network needs to know where to send traffic for a whole subnet, and it does that with an identifier that names the next step along the way.

sections.title: Why a Separate Route Type Is Needed
sections.content:
RFC 7432 defines a MAC/IP Advertisement route, also called route type 2, where a MAC address can be advertised together with an IP address length and an IP address. While a variable IP address length might have been used to indicate the presence of an IP prefix in a route type 2, there are several specific use cases in which using that route type to deliver IP prefixes is not suitable.

The floating IP example shows why. It is necessary to decouple the advertisement of the prefixes from the advertisement of a MAC address of either appliance, otherwise the solution becomes highly inefficient and does not scale. If 1,000 prefixes are advertised from one appliance using route type 2 and the floating IP owner changes to the other appliance, 1,000 routes would be withdrawn by the first appliance and readvertised by the second. If a separate route type is used, the 1,000 routes can be advertised as associated with the floating IP address, and only one route type 2 is needed to advertise the ownership of the floating IP. When the owner changes, a single route type 2 withdrawal or update is required, and the remote gateway does not change any of the 1,000 prefixes, only the address resolution entry for the floating IP.

The new route type 5 therefore decouples IP prefix advertisements from the MAC/IP Advertisement routes. That gives four things. Clean and clear advertisements of IPv4 or IPv6 prefixes in a Network Layer Reachability Information message, without MAC addresses. No need to modify the procedures described in RFC 7432, because the route type is different. A flexible implementation in which the prefix can be linked to different kinds of overlay or underlay index, such as overlay IP addresses, overlay MAC addresses, overlay ESIs, or underlay BGP next hops. And a simple way for an implementation that does not need IP prefixes to discard them, by looking at the route type value.

A node that does not recognize route type 5 will ignore it, so an NVE following this document can still be attached to a broadcast domain where an NVE that ignores route type 5 is attached. In the case where two or more NVEs are attached to different broadcast domains of the same tenant, they MUST support route type 5 for proper inter-subnet forwarding.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping prefixes inside the existing MAC advertisement route would mean re-advertising thousands of routes every time an appliance fails over. A separate route type means one update is enough.

sections.title: The IP Prefix Route Encoding
sections.content:
The BGP EVPN NLRI as defined in RFC 7432 has a route type field of one octet, a length field of one octet, and a variable route-type-specific part. This document defines an additional route type in the IANA EVPN Route Types registry, with value 5 and the description IP Prefix.

An IP Prefix route for IPv4 has the Length field set to 34 and consists of a Route Distinguisher of 8 octets, an Ethernet Segment Identifier of 10 octets, an Ethernet Tag ID of 4 octets, an IP Prefix Length of 1 octet with a value from 0 to 32, an IP Prefix of 4 octets, a gateway IP address of 4 octets, and an MPLS Label of 3 octets. The IPv6 form has the Length field set to 58, with an IP Prefix Length from 0 to 128, and IP Prefix and gateway IP address fields of 16 octets each. The IP prefix and the gateway IP address MUST be from the same address family.

The Route Distinguisher and Ethernet Tag ID MUST be used as defined in RFC 7432 and RFC 8365, and the RD is unique per MAC-VRF or IP-VRF. The MPLS Label field holds either an MPLS label or a VNI, as described in RFC 8365 for the other EVPN route types. The Ethernet Segment Identifier MUST be a non-zero 10-octet identifier if the ESI is used as the Overlay Index, and all bytes zero otherwise. The gateway IP address field encodes a valid IP address used as an Overlay Index, and MUST be all bytes zero if it is not used that way.

The label value SHOULD be zero when sending if a recursive resolution based on an Overlay Index is used. If the received label value is zero, the route MUST contain an Overlay Index and the ingress NVE or PE MUST perform a recursive resolution to find the egress NVE or PE; if the received label is zero and the route does not contain an Overlay Index, it MUST be treated as a withdraw. The RD, Ethernet Tag ID, IP prefix length and IP prefix are part of the route key that BGP uses to compare routes; the other fields are not.
sections.plainLanguage: The route has a fixed shape: the routing identity, a segment identifier, a tag, the prefix and its length, an optional next-hop address and an optional label. The length field tells the receiver how long the whole thing is, 34 bytes for IPv4 and 58 for IPv6.

sections.title: Overlay Indexes and Recursive Resolution
sections.content:
An Overlay Index can be an ESI, an IP address in the tenant's address space, or a MAC address, and it is used by an NVE as the next hop for a given IP prefix. An Overlay Index always needs a recursive route resolution on the NVE or PE that installs the route type 5 into one of its IP-VRFs, so that the NVE knows which egress NVE or PE to forward to. The recursive resolution applies on installation into an IP-VRF and not on BGP propagation, and as a result the egress NVE or PE is not necessarily the NVE that originated the route type 5.

The Overlay Index is carried in the ESI field, the gateway IP field, or the EVPN Router's MAC Extended Community, depending on whether the next hop is an ESI, an IP address or a MAC address in the tenant space, and it is set by local policy at the NVE that originates the route. To make the recursive resolution possible, an NVE that is a possible egress NVE for a given Overlay Index must originate a route advertising itself as the BGP next hop on the path to the system denoted by the Overlay Index.

Concretely, an NVE cannot use the route type 5 in its IP-VRF unless it can recursively resolve the Overlay Index. If the Overlay Index is an ESI, resolution is only possible once the NVE has installed a route type 1 auto-discovery route for that ESI. If it is a gateway IP address, a route type 2 with that IP address in its IP Address field is needed. If it is a MAC address, a route type 2 with that MAC address in its MAC Address field is needed. The route type 1 or route type 2 routes needed for the recursive resolution may arrive before or after the route type 5 route.

Irrespective of the recursive resolution, if there is no IGP or BGP route to the BGP next hop of a route type 5, BGP MUST NOT install the route even if the Overlay Index can be resolved. The ESI and gateway IP fields may both be zero, but they MUST NOT both be non-zero; a route with both non-zero SHOULD be treated as a withdraw. If either is non-zero, the non-zero one is the Overlay Index, whatever the MAC extended community or the label value says; when the gateway IP is the Overlay Index the MAC extended community is ignored if present. A route where the ESI, gateway IP, MAC and label are all zero at the same time SHOULD be treated as a withdraw.
sections.plainLanguage: The next hop in the overlay can be an address, a MAC or a segment identifier, and the receiver has to look that up in another table before it can use the route. If the lookup fails, the route is not used.

sections.title: The Use Cases
sections.content:
The four use cases in the RFC differ only in which kind of Overlay Index they use.

In the tenant system IP address use case, a subnet is dual-homed to two NVEs, and the appliances behind it do not take part in dynamic routing. A gateway IP address is used as the Overlay Index, because the operator knows the appliance IP addresses beforehand while the appliance MAC address is unknown and the appliance ESI is zero. The NVEs learn which gateway IP to use for a given prefix by policy.

In the floating IP address use case, the same 1,000 prefixes are associated with the floating IP address, and a single route type 2 advertises the ownership of that floating IP together with the MAC of the current owner. When the owner changes, only that one route changes.

In the bump-in-the-wire use case, the Overlay Index is an ESI or a MAC address.

In the IP-VRF-to-IP-VRF use case, the Overlay Index can be a gateway IP, a MAC address, or none. The special case where there is no Overlay Index is used when the NVEs are connected by IP overlay tunnels rather than Ethernet overlay tunnels.
sections.plainLanguage: The same route format covers several situations. What changes is the Overlay Index: an appliance address, a segment identifier, a MAC address, or nothing at all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document provides a set of procedures to achieve inter-subnet forwarding across NVEs or PEs attached to a group of broadcast domains that belong to the same tenant or VPN. The security considerations discussed in RFC 7432 apply to intra-subnet forwarding within each of those broadcast domains, and the security considerations in RFC 4364 should also be understood, since the two documents may be used in similar applications.

Contrary to RFC 4364, this document does not describe PE and CE route distribution techniques but rather considers the customer edges as tenant systems or appliances that do not run dynamic routing protocols. The RFC calls this a security advantage, since dynamic routing protocols can be blocked on the attachment circuits, not allowing the tenant to interact with the infrastructure's dynamic routing protocols.

The route type 5 may use a regular BGP next hop for its resolution, or an Overlay Index that requires a recursive resolution to a different EVPN route, a route type 2 or a route type 1. In the latter case, any action that ends up filtering or modifying the route type 2 or route type 1 routes used to convey the Overlay Indexes will modify the resolution of the route type 5, and therefore the forwarding of packets to the remote subnet.
sections.plainLanguage: The tenant's own devices cannot inject routing information, because they never speak a routing protocol. But the route that points at the exit device can be changed by whoever controls the routes that resolve it.

viz.caption: WHAT A SEPARATE ROUTE TYPE BUYS (RFC 9136, SECTION 2.2)

items.title: Clean prefix advertisements
items.text: IPv4 or IPv6 prefixes can be advertised in a reachability message without any MAC address.

items.title: Existing procedures unchanged
items.text: Because the route type differs from the MAC/IP Advertisement route, the procedures in RFC 7432 do not need to be modified.

items.title: Flexible next hops
items.text: A prefix can be linked to overlay IP addresses, overlay MAC addresses, overlay ESIs or underlay BGP next hops.

items.title: Easy to ignore
items.text: An implementation that does not need IP prefixes can discard them by looking at the route type value.

viz.caption: THE KINDS OF TENANT SYSTEM (RFC 9136, SECTION 2.1)

items.title: Virtual machines
items.text: Generate traffic from their own MAC and IP addresses.

items.title: Virtual appliances
items.text: Forward traffic to and from the IP addresses of devices behind them: firewalls, load balancers and NAT devices.

items.title: Appliances without routing
items.text: They do not take part in dynamic routing, so the EVPN NVEs advertise the routes on their behalf.

items.title: Floating addresses
items.text: The same IP address may sit behind two appliances, for example with VRRP, and the owner can change.
